problem: Supervised VLN agents (FAST-MATTN, Airbert, DUET) lose much of their performance moving from seen to unseen environments on REVERIE, and each one is tied to the dataset it was trained on. Before this paper, no work had tried coarse-grained natural-language instruction following (as opposed to template object names, as in CoW) fully zero-shot.
motivation: Every household looks different, and people describe targets with environment-specific language such as 'orange-striped bathroom'. The authors measure a low pairwise average cosine similarity of 0.32 between seen and unseen REVERIE instructions, which suggests training data cannot cover the visuo-linguistic diversity an agent will meet. They therefore ask whether CLIP's zero-shot grounding can drive sequential navigation decisions with no dataset-specific finetuning, relying on CLIP's implicit structural priors about homes (e.g., choosing the doorway view when told 'go to the kitchen').
key_idea: Split a REVERIE instruction into navigation keyphrases and an activity/target phrase, score each of 4 panorama sub-views against the current keyphrase with frozen CLIP, move toward the best-scoring view, and use CLIP-score thresholds (plus a sequence-averaged score for backtracking) to decide when to advance keyphrases, backtrack or stop.
insight: CLIP alone can pick plausible directions from room-level structural priors, but stopping is the bottleneck. Plain CLIP-Nav reaches the target often (val-unseen OSR 27.63) yet rarely stops there (SR 5.79). Adding the SGS-based backtracking in Seq CLIP-Nav nearly triples SR to 14.97 at similar OSR (24.46), which the authors read as backtracking preventing overshoot. The zero-shot agents also show a smaller seen/unseen gap (RCS on SR 17.56 vs 34.52 for DUET). That gap is partly by construction, since nothing is trained on 'seen', and partly because absolute performance is low.
method: Instruction breakdown: split the REVERIE instruction at the conjunction 'and' into a Navigation Component (NC) and an Activity Component (AC). Break the NC into keyphrases either by prepositions or by prompting GPT-3 with 'Break this down into steps.', which preserves temporal order. Keyphrase length is capped because CLIP is sensitive to wording.

CLIP grounding: split each Matterport3D panorama into 4 images of about 90° at a uniform elevation. Frozen CLIP scores the current keyphrase against each image to give a Keyphrase Grounding Score (KGS); the highest-KGS image is the 'CLIP-chosen image'. CLIP also scores the AC against the views, and that score serves as the stop condition.

CLIP-Nav: at each step, move to the closest adjacent navigable node (from the simulator nav graph) visible in the CLIP-chosen image. When the NC grounding score exceeds a threshold, advance to the next keyphrase (intermediate-goal detection). Stop when the AC score exceeds a threshold.
Seq CLIP-Nav: average the KGS of the chosen images over the last n nodes to get a Sequence Grounding Score (SGS = ΣKGS_i / n). A low SGS triggers backtracking a few nodes; a high SGS means continue.
RCS metric: Relative Change in Success = |Seen − Unseen| / max(Seen, Unseen) × 100, computed for SR, OSR and SPL to quantify how consistently a method performs across seen and unseen environments.

setting.backbone: CLIP (frozen, variant not specified) for grounding and decisions; GPT-3 (frozen) optionally for instruction breakdown (the paper does not state which breakdown produced the reported results)
setting.action_space: discrete nav-graph viewpoints (closest navigable node visible in the chosen view), with backtracking in Seq CLIP-Nav
setting.privileged: none beyond the standard nav graph navigable-node lists from the Matterport simulator

numbers_note: Only Table 1 (REVERIE val-seen and val-unseen) is reported. SPL is printed as a fraction (converted to 0-100 here), and for both CLIP methods SPL exceeds SR, which is impossible under standard SPL; treat these SPLs as non-comparable. RCS is a cross-split metric and is attached to the val-unseen entries only. The text also reports per-scan 'Best OSR' on val-unseen: 47.51% (CLIP-Nav) and 48.41% (Seq CLIP-Nav), which are single best house scans, not split-level results. No REVERIE object-grounding metrics (RGS/RGSPL), NE or TL are reported. Whether the full val splits were used is not explicitly stated beyond 'Seen and Unseen validation splits'.
results: On REVERIE val-unseen, the zero-shot Seq CLIP-Nav reaches SR 14.97%, slightly above the supervised REVERIE baseline FAST-MATTN (14.40%) but far below Airbert (27.89%) and DUET (46.98%). Its reported SPL of 0.450 is above DUET's 0.337, but that SPL value exceeds its own SR, so the comparison is suspect. Both CLIP methods have lower seen/unseen gaps (RCS on SR 17.56 and 21.89) than FAST-MATTN (71.50), Airbert (40.67) and DUET (34.52). Backtracking raises unseen SR from 5.79 to 14.97.
limitations: Absolute success is low: 14.97% SR on val-unseen versus 46.98% for DUET. The RCS 'generalization' advantage is largely a by-product of training-free methods having no seen-set benefit, combined with their low absolute performance.
The reported SPL values exceed SR (e.g., 0.450 SPL vs 14.97% SR), so SPL is apparently not the standard definition, and the claimed SOTA SPL is not a valid comparison.

Key details are unspecified: CLIP variant, grounding/stop/backtrack thresholds, n for SGS, and which instruction breakdown (preposition-based or GPT-3) produced the results. Evaluation covers only REVERIE navigation, with no object grounding (RGS).
